chapters.title: The Wall That Crosses a Continent

pages.text: The Great Wall of China is one of the most recognisable structures on earth. It runs across northern China for thousands of kilometres, crossing mountains, deserts, and river valleys, snaking along ridges and clifftops in a path that seems to follow the very shape of the land. It is the longest structure ever built by human hands.

image.note: Panoramic illustration of the Great Wall crossing mountainous terrain

pages.text: The wall is not one wall. It is a collection of walls, towers, fortifications, and barriers built over many centuries by different Chinese states and dynasties. The earliest sections date back more than two thousand years. The most famous and best-preserved sections were built during the Ming Dynasty, between 1368 and 1644 CE.

The total length of all the walls, if measured together, is estimated at more than 21,000 kilometres. The sections most visited by tourists today, near Beijing, were built from brick and stone and are in relatively good condition. Many other sections are made from compressed earth and have eroded over centuries to little more than ridges in the landscape.

The wall was built for one primary purpose: defence. China's northern frontier was repeatedly threatened by nomadic peoples from the steppes of Central Asia, skilled horsemen who raided Chinese settlements and farmland. The wall was designed to slow or stop those raids, to provide watchtowers from which approaching enemies could be spotted, and to create a barrier that would funnel movement through controlled gates.

The first emperor to join the walls into a single system was Qin Shi Huang, who unified China in 221 BCE. He is one of history's most extraordinary figures: the ruler who standardised Chinese writing, weights, measures, and coins, and who was buried with an army of eight thousand life-sized terracotta soldiers, discovered by farmers digging a well in 1974. His wall was built from compressed earth and has largely vanished. The idea of the wall, however, never did.

Over the following centuries, dynasties rose and fell, and each made its own decision about the wall. Some extended it. Some abandoned it. The Tang Dynasty, at the height of its power, felt strong enough to need no wall at all. The Ming Dynasty, after being driven out by Mongol rulers, rebuilt it in stone and brick on a scale never seen before. The wall's history is a mirror of China's confidence: strong when China felt weak, neglected when China felt strong.

The construction of the Great Wall was one of the largest and most costly building projects in human history. It required the labour of millions of workers over many centuries. Many of them were soldiers, who built the wall as part of their military service. Many were conscripted peasants, ordered to leave their farms and families and travel to the frontier to work. Many died there.

The working conditions were brutal. The wall was built through some of the most inhospitable terrain in China: high mountain passes where temperatures fell far below freezing in winter, dry deserts where water was scarce, remote valleys far from any settlement. Workers who died were sometimes buried within the wall itself. Chinese legend calls the Great Wall the longest cemetery in the world.

The materials varied depending on what was available locally. In areas with good stone, the wall was built from stone blocks. In desert areas, it was built from compressed earth, sometimes mixed with reeds or straw for binding. In the later Ming sections, grey brick, fired in kilns near the site, was the primary material. The wall adapted to its environment, which is part of why it looks different in different places.

pages.text: The watchtowers are among the most distinctive features of the Ming wall. They were placed at regular intervals, close enough that a signal fire lit in one tower could be seen from the next. A chain of signal fires could carry news of an approaching enemy from the frontier to Beijing in a matter of hours, far faster than any messenger on horseback could travel.

The bricks of the Ming wall carry a quality control system that modern engineers admire. Many are stamped with the name of the workshop that made them and the date of manufacture. If a section of wall failed, inspectors could trace the faulty bricks back to their source, and the makers were held responsible. Some historians credit this accountability for the extraordinary durability of the Ming sections. Six hundred years later, the stamps are still legible.

Supplying the builders was a war of its own. Grain, tools, and brick had to be carried up mountains where no cart could travel. Legend says that goats were sometimes loaded with bricks and driven up the slopes. Lime mortar was mixed, according to tradition, with sticky rice, and modern laboratory tests have confirmed it: the rice starch made the mortar stronger and more water resistant. The recipe was a state secret of its time.

The Great Wall was not always effective as a military barrier. Nomadic armies found ways around it, through it, and sometimes simply through gates whose guards had been bribed. In 1644, the Ming Dynasty fell not to a foreign invasion across the wall but to internal rebellion, which then allowed the Manchu people from the north to enter China and establish the Qing Dynasty.

Despite its limitations as a military barrier, the wall had enormous symbolic importance. It represented the boundary between the Chinese world and the world beyond. On one side was civilisation, as the Chinese understood it: settled farming communities, cities, law, and culture. On the other side was the unknown, the threatening, the other. The wall was as much a statement of identity as a military structure.

The section of the wall near the Juyong Pass, north of Beijing, was the most heavily trafficked and most fought over. It is here that the wall is widest and most elaborately built, with stairs, ramparts, and multiple defensive layers. It is also here that some of the most impressive surviving sections can be visited today.

The most famous story about the wall is also false: that it is the only human-made structure visible from space. Astronauts have repeatedly reported that it is not visible from orbit with the naked eye. The wall is long, but it is narrow, and it is built from materials the same colour as the land around it. The myth appeared in print before anyone had ever been to space, and it has outlived every correction. Myths about the wall are almost as durable as the wall itself.

The wall that repelled armies could not repel one visitor: Genghis Khan. In the early thirteenth century, the Mongol leader's armies swept past and through the fortifications, sometimes by finding gaps, sometimes by persuading gatekeepers to open the doors. His grandson Kublai Khan ruled all of China. The lesson was not lost on later dynasties: a wall is only as strong as the people defending it, and no wall defends itself.

The Great Wall of China was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. It is one of the most visited tourist destinations in the world, attracting millions of visitors every year, many of them to the restored sections near Beijing at Badaling and Mutianyu.

The condition of the wall varies enormously. The heavily visited sections near Beijing are well maintained and have been significantly restored. In more remote areas, the wall is crumbling or has disappeared entirely. Erosion, farming, and the removal of bricks for building material have damaged or destroyed large sections. Conservation organisations estimate that only about thirty percent of the Ming wall remains in good condition.

The wall continues to inspire. It appears on the Chinese national emblem, on banknotes, and in the imagery used to represent China all over the world. It is studied by historians, archaeologists, engineers, and architects. It has been the subject of more books, documentaries, and paintings than almost any other structure on earth.

And yet, for all its fame, much about the wall remains unknown. The exact number of people who died building it cannot be calculated. The precise engineering methods used for some sections are still debated. New sections are still being discovered in remote areas. The Great Wall of China, like the Great Wall of Benin, is still giving up its secrets.

Conservation of the wall today is a race against time, weather, and human carelessness. Farmers once dismantled sections for building material. Tourists carve names into ancient brick. Sandstorms wear down the earthen sections of the west. China has passed laws protecting the wall, and volunteers patrol remote stretches, reporting damage and clearing rubbish. The Great Wall took two thousand years to build. Keeping it standing may prove to be a project every bit as long.
